# Industrial Services Unit: Turnaround-or-Exit Assessment & Decision Framework

## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This assessment provides a diagnostic framework and action plan for a chronically unprofitable industrial-services business unit within a diversified group. The situation is critical: **three years of losses despite cost-cutting suggests structural problems (pricing, market positioning, or customer mix) that cost-cutting alone cannot fix.** The one-year deadline requires immediate diagnosis and parallel path planning.

**Core thesis:** Losses are likely **execution-driven + structural misalignment**, not inevitable. Cost-cutting has failed because it treated symptoms (high costs) rather than root causes (low pricing, wrong customer mix, or service model broken for current market). A 12-month recovery plan can succeed if:

1. **Root cause diagnosis is completed within 60 days** (not assumptions; actual data on margins by customer/service line)
2. **Customer segmentation and repricing are aggressive within 90 days** (not incremental; 10–20% price increases for high-value customers)
3. **Service lines are pruned ruthlessly** (exit lowest-margin work; consolidate delivery)
4. **Exit option is pursued in parallel** (don't wait 12 months to explore divestment; start now to have leverage)

**Success probability: 60–70% if execution is disciplined; 20–30% if board/leadership hesitate.**

---

## 1. DIAGNOSTIC FRAMEWORK: ROOT CAUSES OF SUSTAINED LOSSES

### 1.1 Symptoms vs. Root Causes

```
WHAT THE BOARD SEES (SYMPTOMS):
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Year 1 Loss: -$5M (on $50M revenue = -10% margin)
Year 2 Loss: -$4.5M (on $45M revenue = -10% margin) ← Cost-cutting didn't move needle
Year 3 Loss: -$4.2M (on $40M revenue = -10.5% margin) ← Shrinking revenue + fixed costs

Visible problems:
├─ Declining order book (customers not renewing/expanding)
├─ Best managers leaving (why stay in a loss-making unit?)
├─ Two restructuring attempts failed (cost cuts didn't translate to profitability)
├─ Business still unprofitable despite aggressive cost control
└─ Board patience exhausted (one year to fix or sell)

DIAGNOSIS: Why did cost-cutting fail?
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ROOT CAUSE HYPOTHESIS #1: PRICING BELOW MARGINAL COST
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

What it means:
├─ Some/all customer segments are priced so low that you lose money on every incremental sale
├─ Volume growth would make losses WORSE, not better
├─ Cost-cutting fails because the problem isn't cost; it's revenue
├─ Common in industrial services: Long customer relationships → pricing erosion over time
│                                   "We've always charged you X" → X is now below cost

Red flags for this cause:
├─ Orders are being won but don't improve profit (or worsen it)
├─ Sales team claims "customers are price-sensitive; we can't raise rates"
├─ Cost-cutting revealed fixed overhead but variable costs are still underwater
├─ Competitors quoting 20–30% higher prices (indicates you're dumping)
├─ Customer win rate is high but profitability per customer is negative
├─ Large customers are least profitable (volume discounts + high service expectations)
└─ Margin analysis by customer shows pattern: Biggest customers = biggest losses

Example:
├─ Service line A: Field maintenance contracts
│  ├─ Customer base: 50 customers, average $800K revenue per customer
│  ├─ Contract pricing: $80–100/hour labor (industry standard: $120–150/hour)
│  ├─ Service model: On-call, responsive (high overhead cost)
│  ├─ Actual labor cost: $65/hour; loaded cost: $95/hour
│  ├─ Margin per service hour: $80–100 revenue, $95 cost = NEGATIVE $15–(-$15) per hour
│  ├─ Why it happened: Contracts were priced 5–10 years ago; never repriced despite inflation
│  └─ Impact: Every contract renewed is a loss; every new contract deepens hole

ROOT CAUSE HYPOTHESIS #2: WRONG CUSTOMER MIX / CUSTOMER CONCENTRATION
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

What it means:
├─ High-value customer base has been replaced by low-margin accounts
├─ Unit is chasing volume (customers who are hard to serve, price-sensitive, low-margin)
├─ Best customers have left (defection risk); unit is retaining worst customers
├─ Possibly the core customer base for group has become unprofitable (external factors?)

Red flags for this cause:
├─ Customer base has shifted: Fewer large integrated customers; more spot/transactional work
├─ NPS or retention metrics show declining satisfaction (customers don't value service)
├─ Best customers (highest profit margin) have left in last 3 years
├─ Remaining customers are sticky (hard to serve) but price-sensitive
├─ Market share in profitable segments has declined
├─ Service requests increasingly commoditized (customers can get it cheaper elsewhere)
├─ Customer concentration: Revenue is spread wide but margins are concentrated in few (leaving accounts)
└─ Competitor activity: Competitors are winning your profitable customers

Example:
├─ Customer segment A (Traditional industrial): 30% of volume, 70% of profit
│  ├─ Lost 40% of customer base (5 of 12) over 3 years to competitors
│  ├─ Reason: Competitors offered lower price + better technology integration
│  ├─ Remaining customers are price-shopping
│
├─ Customer segment B (Specialty/niche): 20% of volume, 20% of profit
│  ├─ Stable (few customers, sticky)
│  ├─ Profitable but small (not enough to offset losses)
│
└─ Customer segment C (Transactional/ad hoc): 50% of volume, 10% of profit
   ├─ Growing (unit chasing volume to offset segment A losses)
   ├─ Unprofitable (low prices, high service requests, low margin)
   ├─ Unit is cannibalizing itself: Serving C customers to cover A losses

ROOT CAUSE HYPOTHESIS #3: SERVICE MODEL / DELIVERY STRUCTURE BROKEN
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

What it means:
├─ The way service is being delivered (fixed costs, staffing model, operations) doesn't match market reality
├─ Market expects different service model (faster response, more flexibility, technology-enabled)
├─ Unit's delivery model is built for old market; can't scale profitably in new market
├─ Competitors have modernized; your unit is obsolete operationally

Red flags for this cause:
├─ High fixed overhead (field office network, minimum staffing) not justified by revenue
├─ Customer requests increasingly for "on-demand" vs. "contracted" service
├─ Competitors can deliver faster/cheaper using different model (gig model, tech platform, hub-and-spoke)
├─ Utilization rates are low: Field technicians are 60–70% utilized (overhead not covered)
├─ Complexity in operations (multiple service centers, duplicate overhead, poor coordination)
├─ Technology lag: Competitors have dispatching/scheduling platforms; you don't
├─ Lead times are high (customers waiting days; competitors deliver same day)
├─ Rework/quality issues are high (driving up cost per service)
└─ Scaling is hard: Adding customers = adding fixed costs (can't achieve leverage)

Example:
├─ Current model: 8 regional service centers, each with minimum staff
│  ├─ Fixed cost per center: $1M/year (rent, management, equipment)
│  ├─ Total fixed overhead: $8M/year
│  ├─ Revenue per center: $5M (on average)
│  ├─ Margin required to break even: $8M / $40M = 20% (can't achieve)
│
├─ Competitor model: 2 centralized hubs + mobile workforce
│  ├─ Fixed cost: $2M/year (hubs)
│  ├─ Variable cost: Higher (mileage, real-time dispatch coordination)
│  ├─ Revenue same: $40M
│  ├─ Margin required: ~12% (achievable)
│
└─ Result: You have 4x the fixed overhead per dollar of revenue; can't compete on price

ROOT CAUSE HYPOTHESIS #4: PRODUCT / SERVICE LINE DETERIORATION
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

What it means:
├─ Specific service lines (product categories) are unprofitable and dragging down unit
├─ Some service lines are commoditized; others are still defensible
├─ Cost-cutting = cutting uniform across unit; should be cutting by service line
├─ Some service lines should be exited entirely; others should be scaled

Red flags for this cause:
├─ Margin analysis by service line shows 2–3 lines are highly profitable, rest are negative
├─ Unprofitable lines are declining anyway (market is shrinking)
├─ Profitable lines are growing (market opportunity is here, not there)
├─ Unit is "bundling" unprofitable service with profitable ones (customers want bundled service)
├─ Competitors have exited unprofitable lines; you're hanging on (hoping for recovery)
├─ Service lines require different go-to-market (sales, pricing, customer base), not unified
├─ Consolidation opportunity: Small teams doing similar work across multiple service lines
└─ Automation potential: Some service lines can be partially automated; others can't

Example:
├─ Service line A (Preventive maintenance): 30% of revenue, 8% margin
│  ├─ Commodity market; pricing pressure from competitors and customers
│  ├─ High fixed cost (technician base, scheduling, customer relationships)
│  ├─ Declining order book (customers self-servicing)
│  └─ Recommendation: Exit or radically restructure (move to lower-touch, lower-cost model)
│
├─ Service line B (Emergency/reactive repair): 40% of revenue, -5% margin
│  ├─ Customers expect fast response (drives high cost)
│  ├─ Pricing power is weak ("emergency" doesn't justify premium price in customer minds)
│  ├─ Demand is volatile (can't plan staffing)
│  └─ Recommendation: Restructure pricing (customer pays for speed/guarantee) or exit
│
├─ Service line C (Specialized technical services): 20% of revenue, 22% margin
│  ├─ High-skilled technicians (scarce, expensive, good margin)
│  ├─ Customers willing to pay premium (mission-critical, differentiated)
│  ├─ Growing demand (customers need more specialization)
│  └─ Recommendation: Scale this; invest in talent, pricing
│
└─ Service line D (Asset management / monitoring): 10% of revenue, -2% margin
   ├─ Tech-enabled service (software + hardware)
   ├─ Customer expectations: 24/7 availability, real-time alerts
   ├─ Current delivery model: Manual monitoring (can't meet customer expectations, unprofitable)
   └─ Recommendation: Either transform to tech platform (invest) or exit

ROOT CAUSE HYPOTHESIS #5: EXECUTION / OPERATIONAL EXCELLENCE ISSUES
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

What it means:
├─ Pricing and customer mix might be OK, but operational execution is poor
├─ High rework, waste, inefficiency, or overstaffing is destroying margins
├─ Unit has lost discipline in cost control / operational rigor
├─ Best managers leaving = management depth missing = execution quality declining
├─ Culture of "do whatever it takes to win the deal" has eroded margins

Red flags for this cause:
├─ Rework/quality metrics are high vs. competitors
├─ Labor utilization rates are low (too much non-billable time)
├─ Absenteeism/turnover is high (team is disengaged, burned out)
├─ Project cost overruns are common (schedule slips, scope creep)
├─ Customer complaints about service quality are increasing
├─ Inventory waste is high (dead stock, shrink)
├─ Procurement is inefficient (not getting competitive pricing)
└─ Best performers are leaving (those who care about quality/standards)

ROOT CAUSE HYPOTHESIS #6: MARKET / EXTERNAL STRUCTURAL DECLINE
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

What it means:
├─ The industrial-services market itself is in decline
├─ Customer demand has shifted (they need different services, or less service)
├─ Disruption has changed what customers buy (automation, insourcing, different service models)
├─ Unit is in a shrinking market; no cost-cutting will fix market decline

Red flags for this cause:
├─ Entire market is declining (not just your unit; competitors also losing share)
├─ Customer base is shrinking (consolidation, automation, outsourcing)
├─ New entrants are disrupting (gig model, tech platforms, direct-to-consumer)
├─ Price compression is industry-wide (not just your pricing problem)
├─ Order book is declining across all service lines (not specific to weak lines)
├─ Winning new customers is increasingly hard (even after price cuts)
├─ Customer churn is accelerating (customers going direct, to competitors, or reducing spend)
├─ Technology displacement (robots, AI, IoT are replacing manual industrial services)
└─ Best customers' economics are deteriorating (they're buying less because their economics are bad)

Example:
├─ Industrial base in your region has been declining 3–5% annually for 10 years
├─ Manufacturing customers are automating (fewer breakdowns, less maintenance)
├─ New service model (predictive maintenance via IoT) is replacing reactive maintenance
├─ Your unit is still offering reactive 24/7 maintenance (expensive, low demand)
├─ All competitors are in same situation (but some are pivoting to tech-enabled services)

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
```

### 1.2 Diagnostic Roadmap: 60-Day Root Cause Assessment

**Goal:** Move from hypothesis to fact-based diagnosis of where losses are coming from. This is non-negotiable; don't proceed with turnaround plan without clear diagnosis.

```
PHASE 1: DATA COLLECTION & SEGMENTATION (Days 1–20)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Activity 1.1: Gross Margin Analysis by Customer & Service Line
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Pull data from finance/operations:
├─ Revenue by customer (last 24 months)
├─ Direct cost of service by customer (labor, materials, subcontracts)
├─ Gross margin by customer (revenue - direct costs) / revenue
├─ Service lines associated with each customer (many customers use multiple services)
├─ Revenue by service line (isolated from customer data)
├─ Direct cost by service line
├─ Gross margin by service line

Output: Two matrices:
├─ Matrix A: Customer profitability map
│  ├─ Rank 50 largest customers by revenue
│  ├─ Show gross margin for each
│  ├─ Identify customers with negative or <5% margin
│  ├─ Identify customers with >25% margin (your profitable anchor customers)
│  └─ Show trend (margin improving/declining year over year)
│
└─ Matrix B: Service line profitability map
   ├─ Rank service lines by revenue
   ├─ Show gross margin for each
   ├─ Identify unprofitable service lines (negative or <10% margin)
   ├─ Identify profitable service lines (>20% margin)
   └─ Show trend (growing/declining)

Key insight: If 20% of customers = 100% of profit, then problem is customer mix + pricing.
             If service lines show wide variance (some +30%, some -10%), problem is portfolio mix.
             If all customers/lines show declining margins, problem is either pricing or delivery model.

Activity 1.2: Customer Concentration & Churn Analysis
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Pull data:
├─ Top 20 customers: Revenue, margin, whether they've grown, shrunk, or stayed flat
├─ Customer wins in last 24 months: How many, at what size, with what terms
├─ Customer losses in last 24 months: How many, at what size, for what reasons
├─ Customer churn rate: Count of customers lost / average active customer base
├─ Reason for churn (interview sales team, account managers):
│  ├─ Price (customer found cheaper alternative)
│  ├─ Service quality (customer dissatisfied with service)
│  ├─ Competitor displacement (lost to specific competitor)
│  ├─ Customer consolidation/closure (customer went out of business or merged)
│  ├─ Insourcing (customer decided to do in-house instead)
│  └─ Not specified (customer stopped buying, no clear reason)
│
└─ High-value customer retention: Separate analysis for top 25 customers
   ├─ How many have been with you 5+ years (sticky)
   ├─ How many were gained in last 3 years (new wins)
   ├─ Churn trend: Are you losing high-value or low-value customers?

Key insight: If losing high-value customers to price, you have pricing problem + possibly delivery problem.
             If high churn but low deflection, you have customer satisfaction/market problem.
             If new customer wins aren't sticking, you have sales/onboarding problem.

Activity 1.3: Pricing vs. Market Analysis
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Research competitor pricing:
├─ For each service line, identify 3–5 key competitors
├─ Research/request pricing for identical service scope
├─ Compare your pricing to competitor pricing (percentage difference)
├─ For customers you've lost, ask: "What did competitor quote you?"
├─ For customers you've won, ask: "What did you expect to pay vs. what we quoted?"

Output:
├─ Pricing vs. market sheet:
│  ├─ Service line A: You $100/hour; Market: $130/hour (30% BELOW market = pricing problem)
│  ├─ Service line B: You $80/hour; Market: $80/hour (AT market = execution problem if unprofitable)
│  ├─ Service line C: You $200/hour; Market: $180/hour (10% ABOVE market but profitable = differentiated)
│  └─ Service line D: You $60/hour; Market: $90/hour (33% BELOW market = likely dumping)
│
└─ Pricing history (pull from CRM):
   ├─ When were prices last increased?
   ├─ Were increases across the board or by customer?
   ├─ How much resistance to price increases?
   └─ Are old customers locked in at old rates?

Key insight: If your pricing is 20–30% below market, root cause is clear: PRICING PROBLEM.
             If pricing is at market but margins are negative, root cause is DELIVERY/EXECUTION PROBLEM.

Activity 1.4: Customer Switching Cost & Stickiness Analysis
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

For top 20 customers, assess:
├─ How integrated is your service into their operations?
│  ├─ Critical (customer depends on you to operate): Switching cost = HIGH
│  ├─ Important (customer would be disrupted but could manage): Switching cost = MEDIUM
│  ├─ Useful (customer could easily replace with competitor): Switching cost = LOW
│
├─ How long have they been customers? (Longer = more integrated = higher switching cost)
├─ How many internal resources do they dedicate to managing relationship?
├─ Do they use your service for multiple needs (bundled) or single need (commoditized)?
├─ What would it cost them to switch? (Time, disruption, training, qualification of new vendor)
└─ Is there contractual lock-in? (Long-term contracts, penalties for early termination)

Key insight: High-switching-cost customers should be protected (priority for retention, price increases reasonable).
             Low-switching-cost customers are vulnerable to churn (need service excellence or pricing advantage).

Activity 1.5: Overhead & Fixed Cost Analysis
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Pull from finance:
├─ Headcount by function (sales, operations, management, admin)
├─ Headcount by location (regional centers, field, corporate)
├─ Headcount trend (how many people were there 3 years ago, now)
├─ Compensation costs (wages, benefits, overhead)
├─ Fixed costs by location: Rent, utilities, facilities, insurance
├─ Fixed costs by function: Corporate allocation, shared services
├─ Fixed costs that vary with revenue (proportional) vs. fixed costs (lump sum)

Output:
├─ Fixed cost as % of revenue:
│  ├─ 3 years ago: Fixed cost = $X, Revenue = $Y, Ratio = X/Y
│  ├─ Today: Fixed cost = $X', Revenue = $Y', Ratio = X'/Y' (likely HIGHER if revenue declined)
│  └─ Indicates: Revenue declined but fixed costs didn't → margin compression
│
├─ Overhead per customer (by size):
│  ├─ Average large customer: $800K revenue, needs dedicated account manager + support (overhead = $100K)
│  ├─ Average medium customer: $200K revenue, needs part-time support (overhead = $20K)
│  ├─ Average small customer: $50K revenue, minimal overhead support (overhead = $5K)
│  └─ Indicates: If customer base has shifted to smaller customers, overhead per customer is too high
│
├─ Delivery cost by model:
│  ├─ On-call/responsive service: High fixed cost (minimum crew, ready to respond)
│  ├─ Scheduled/contracted service: Medium fixed cost (crews scheduled, not always on-call)
│  ├─ Project-based service: Low fixed cost (crews assigned as needed)
│  └─ Indicates: If customer demand has shifted from scheduled to transactional, your model is misaligned
│
└─ Utilization rates (by location/team):
   ├─ Field technician utilization: What % of their time is billable to customer (vs. travel, admin, training)?
   ├─ If <70%, you have overhead problem (costs too high for revenue generated)
   ├─ If 50–60%, you have model problem (can't achieve profitability with this model)
   └─ Benchmark: Profitable service businesses run at 75–85% utilization

Key insight: If fixed costs have stayed flat while revenue declined 20%, margin compression is explained.
             If customer base has shifted to smaller customers, overhead per customer is too high.
             If utilization rates are <70%, delivery model needs restructuring.

DELIVERABLE (Day 20): Root Cause Hypothesis Summary
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Based on Phase 1 data, rank the root causes:

1. PRIMARY DRIVER (the #1 thing causing losses):
   ├─ If customer margin analysis shows 20% of customers = 100% of profit, and unit is chasing volume in low-margin
   │  customer base → PRIMARY DRIVER = CUSTOMER MIX & PRICING
   │
   ├─ If service line analysis shows 2–3 lines are profitable and rest are underwater → PRIMARY DRIVER = PORTFOLIO MIX
   │
   ├─ If pricing is 20–30% below market → PRIMARY DRIVER = PRICING PROBLEM
   │
   ├─ If pricing is at market but utilization is <70% and fixed costs are high → PRIMARY DRIVER = DELIVERY MODEL
   │
   └─ If all metrics show decline (shrinking market, declining margins, declining volume) → PRIMARY DRIVER = MARKET DECLINE
       (This is the hardest to fix; exit may be only option)

2. SECONDARY DRIVERS (contributing factors):
   ├─ Execution issues (rework, inefficiency, waste)
   ├─ Organizational decay (best managers leaving, culture deteriorating)
   ├─ Technology lag (competitors have platforms, you don't)
   └─ Product mix (unprofitable service lines need to be exited)

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PHASE 2: DEEP DIVE BY ROOT CAUSE (Days 21–45)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Based on Phase 1 diagnosis, execute deep dive:

IF PRIMARY DRIVER = CUSTOMER MIX & PRICING:
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Activity 2.1: Repricing opportunity analysis
├─ For each profitable customer segment, model: "What if we raised prices by 10%, 15%, 20%?"
├─ Estimate churn impact (how many customers would leave at each price increase?)
├─ Calculate net revenue impact (revenue increase minus churn loss)
├─ Example:
│  ├─ Segment A (high-switching-cost customers): 20 customers, $800K avg revenue, 40% gross margin
│  │  ├─ Current total: $16M revenue, $6.4M gross profit
│  │  ├─ If raise price 15%, lose 1 customer (5% churn):
│  │  │  ├─ New total: $16M * 1.15 * 0.95 = $17.48M revenue
│  │  │  ├─ New profit (40% margin): $6.99M gross profit
│  │  │  ├─ Gain: +$600K gross profit from single price move
│  │  └─ Recommendation: EXECUTE this price increase (customers can tolerate it; high switching cost protects you)
│  │
│  └─ Segment B (price-sensitive customers): 60 customers, $200K avg revenue, 12% gross margin
│     ├─ Current total: $12M revenue, $1.44M gross profit
│     ├─ If raise price 10%, lose 10% of customers (6 customers):
│     │  ├─ New total: $12M * 1.10 * 0.90 = $11.88M revenue
│     │  ├─ New profit (15% margin, improved by consolidation): $1.78M
│     │  ├─ Gain: +$340K gross profit (but lost 6 customers)
│     │  └─ Recommendation: SELECTIVE reprice + consolidate operations (exit lowest-margin customers to improve overall mix)
│     │
│     └─ Alternative: Exit lowest-margin customers in segment (30 customers, $100K avg, 5% margin)
│        ├─ Revenue impact: -$3M
│        ├─ Profit impact: -$150K (they were barely breaking even)
│        ├─ But reduces overhead allocation to remaining customers → improves overall margin to 15%
│        └─ Recommendation: PRUNE customer base; focus on profitable accounts

Activity 2.2: Customer segment profitability mapping
├─ Identify customer segments (by industry, size, geography, service mix)
├─ Calculate segment-level metrics:
│  ├─ Revenue, gross margin, contribution margin (gross margin - allocated overhead)
│  ├─ Churn rate, NPS, switching cost
│  ├─ Competitive intensity (how many competitors do they buy from?)
│  └─ Growth potential (expanding or contracting customers?)
│
└─ Rank segments by profit and opportunity:
   ├─ TIER 1 (Defend & Grow): Profitable, sticky, growing → increase prices 10–15%; invest in growth
   ├─ TIER 2 (Optimize & Consolidate): Profitable but slow-growing → increase prices 5–10%; consolidate to improve efficiency
   ├─ TIER 3 (Restructure or Exit): Unprofitable or barely profitable → either restructure (new pricing/model) or exit
   └─ TIER 4 (Exit): Unprofitable, low margin, declining → EXIT; reallocate overhead to profitable segments

IF PRIMARY DRIVER = DELIVERY MODEL / FIXED COSTS:
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Activity 2.3: Service delivery model redesign
├─ Current model: Describe how service is currently delivered (staffing, locations, response model, customer interaction)
├─ Cost structure: Fixed costs per location, variable costs per service delivery
├─ Constraint: What customer expectations drive the current model? (24/7 response, on-call, local presence?)
├─ Market shifts: Have customer expectations changed? (Less on-call, more scheduled, more tech-enabled?)
│
├─ Scenario modeling: Test alternative models:
│  │
│  ├─ Model A (Current): 8 regional centers, $8M fixed cost, 70% utilization
│  │  ├─ Revenue: $40M at 20% margin = $8M gross profit
│  │  ├─ Contribution after fixed costs: $0M (break-even, barely)
│  │  └─ Issue: Scale problem; adding revenue doesn't add margin
│  │
│  ├─ Model B (Hub & Spoke): 2 regional hubs + mobile workforce
│  │  ├─ Fixed cost: $3M (hubs) + higher mileage/coordination ($1M) = $4M
│  │  ├─ Utilization: 75% (improved with better scheduling)
│  │  ├─ Revenue same: $40M
│  │  ├─ Gross profit (20% margin): $8M
│  │  ├─ Contribution after fixed costs: $4M (positive!)
│  │  └─ Trade-off: Slower response time for some customers; may lose customers requiring instant response
│  │
│  ├─ Model C (On-Demand / Gig): Partner with contractors for field delivery; retain core team for customer management + quality
│  │  ├─ Fixed cost: $2M (core team, admin, dispatch)
│  │  ├─ Variable cost: Higher (contractor markups) but scales with volume
│  │  ├─ Utilization: 85% (no idle capacity; variable cost = variable supply)
│  │  ├─ Revenue same: $40M, but margin squeezed to 18% (contractor premiums)
│  │  ├─ Gross profit: $7.2M
│  │  ├─ Contribution after fixed costs: $5.2M (best leverage)
│  │  └─ Trade-off: Quality control, customer consistency (contractors may not maintain your standards)
│  │
│  └─ Model D (Tech-Enabled / Self-Service Hybrid): Customer portals, IoT monitoring, predictive maintenance, only dispatch when critical
│     ├─ Fixed cost: $3M (tech platform, core team, support) - NEEDS INVESTMENT
│     ├─ Variable cost: Lower (fewer emergency calls, more predictive work)
│     ├─ Revenue: Could grow to $50M (customers do more with you because model is more efficient for them)
│     ├─ Margin: 25–30% (efficiency gains)
│     ├─ Contribution after fixed costs: $9M (best profitability IF you can execute)

# Industrial Services Unit: Turnaround-or-Exit Assessment & Decision Framework

## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This assessment provides a diagnostic framework and action plan for a chronically unprofitable industrial-services business unit within a diversified group. The situation is critical: **three years of losses despite cost-cutting suggests structural problems (pricing, market positioning, or customer mix) that cost-cutting alone cannot fix.** The one-year deadline requires immediate diagnosis and parallel path planning.

**Core thesis:** Losses are likely **execution-driven + structural misalignment**, not inevitable. Cost-cutting has failed because it treated symptoms (high costs) rather than root causes (low pricing, wrong customer mix, or service model broken for current market). A 12-month recovery plan can succeed if:

1. **Root cause diagnosis is completed within 60 days** (not assumptions; actual data on margins by customer/service line)
2. **Customer segmentation and repricing are aggressive within 90 days** (not incremental; 10–20% price increases for high-value customers)
3. **Service lines are pruned ruthlessly** (exit lowest-margin work; consolidate delivery)
4. **Exit option is pursued in parallel** (don't wait 12 months to explore divestment; start now to have leverage)

**Success probability: 60–70% if execution is disciplined; 20–30% if board/leadership hesitate.**

---

## 1. DIAGNOSTIC FRAMEWORK: ROOT CAUSES OF SUSTAINED LOSSES

### 1.1 Symptoms vs. Root Causes

```
WHAT THE BOARD SEES (SYMPTOMS):
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Year 1 Loss: -$5M (on $50M revenue = -10% margin)
Year 2 Loss: -$4.5M (on $45M revenue = -10% margin) ← Cost-cutting didn't move needle
Year 3 Loss: -$4.2M (on $40M revenue = -10.5% margin) ← Shrinking revenue + fixed costs

Visible problems:
├─ Declining order book (customers not renewing/expanding)
├─ Best managers leaving (why stay in a loss-making unit?)
├─ Two restructuring attempts failed (cost cuts didn't translate to profitability)
├─ Business still unprofitable despite aggressive cost control
└─ Board patience exhausted (one year to fix or sell)

DIAGNOSIS: Why did cost-cutting fail?
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ROOT CAUSE HYPOTHESIS #1: PRICING BELOW MARGINAL COST
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

What it means:
├─ Some/all customer segments are priced so low that you lose money on every incremental sale
├─ Volume growth would make losses WORSE, not better
├─ Cost-cutting fails because the problem isn't cost; it's revenue
├─ Common in industrial services: Long customer relationships → pricing erosion over time
│                                   "We've always charged you X" → X is now below cost

Red flags for this cause:
├─ Orders are being won but don't improve profit (or worsen it)
├─ Sales team claims "customers are price-sensitive; we can't raise rates"
├─ Cost-cutting revealed fixed overhead but variable costs are still underwater
├─ Competitors quoting 20–30% higher prices (indicates you're dumping)
├─ Customer win rate is high but profitability per customer is negative
├─ Large customers are least profitable (volume discounts + high service expectations)
└─ Margin analysis by customer shows pattern: Biggest customers = biggest losses

Example:
├─ Service line A: Field maintenance contracts
│  ├─ Customer base: 50 customers, average $800K revenue per customer
│  ├─ Contract pricing: $80–100/hour labor (industry standard: $120–150/hour)
│  ├─ Service model: On-call, responsive (high overhead cost)
│  ├─ Actual labor cost: $65/hour; loaded cost: $95/hour
│  ├─ Margin per service hour: $80–100 revenue, $95 cost = NEGATIVE $15–(-$15) per hour
│  ├─ Why it happened: Contracts were priced 5–10 years ago; never repriced despite inflation
│  └─ Impact: Every contract renewed is a loss; every new contract deepens hole

ROOT CAUSE HYPOTHESIS #2: WRONG CUSTOMER MIX / CUSTOMER CONCENTRATION
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

What it means:
├─ High-value customer base has been replaced by low-margin accounts
├─ Unit is chasing volume (customers who are hard to serve, price-sensitive, low-margin)
├─ Best customers have left (defection risk); unit is retaining worst customers
├─ Possibly the core customer base for group has become unprofitable (external factors?)

Red flags for this cause:
├─ Customer base has shifted: Fewer large integrated customers; more spot/transactional work
├─ NPS or retention metrics show declining satisfaction (customers don't value service)
├─ Best customers (highest profit margin) have left in last 3 years
├─ Remaining customers are sticky (hard to serve) but price-sensitive
├─ Market share in profitable segments has declined
├─ Service requests increasingly commoditized (customers can get it cheaper elsewhere)
├─ Customer concentration: Revenue is spread wide but margins are concentrated in few (leaving accounts)
└─ Competitor activity: Competitors are winning your profitable customers

Example:
├─ Customer segment A (Traditional industrial): 30% of volume, 70% of profit
│  ├─ Lost 40% of customer base (5 of 12) over 3 years to competitors
│  ├─ Reason: Competitors offered lower price + better technology integration
│  ├─ Remaining customers are price-shopping
│
├─ Customer segment B (Specialty/niche): 20% of volume, 20% of profit
│  ├─ Stable (few customers, sticky)
│  ├─ Profitable but small (not enough to offset losses)
│
└─ Customer segment C (Transactional/ad hoc): 50% of volume, 10% of profit
   ├─ Growing (unit chasing volume to offset segment A losses)
   ├─ Unprofitable (low prices, high service requests, low margin)
   ├─ Unit is cannibalizing itself: Serving C customers to cover A losses

ROOT CAUSE HYPOTHESIS #3: SERVICE MODEL / DELIVERY STRUCTURE BROKEN
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

What it means:
├─ The way service is being delivered (fixed costs, staffing model, operations) doesn't match market reality
├─ Market expects different service model (faster response, more flexibility, technology-enabled)
├─ Unit's delivery model is built for old market; can't scale profitably in new market
├─ Competitors have modernized; your unit is obsolete operationally

Red flags for this cause:
├─ High fixed overhead (field office network, minimum staffing) not justified by revenue
├─ Customer requests increasingly for "on-demand" vs. "contracted" service
├─ Competitors can deliver faster/cheaper using different model (gig model, tech platform, hub-and-spoke)
├─ Utilization rates are low: Field technicians are 60–70% utilized (overhead not covered)
├─ Complexity in operations (multiple service centers, duplicate overhead, poor coordination)
├─ Technology lag: Competitors have dispatching/scheduling platforms; you don't
├─ Lead times are high (customers waiting days; competitors deliver same day)
├─ Rework/quality issues are high (driving up cost per service)
└─ Scaling is hard: Adding customers = adding fixed costs (can't achieve leverage)

Example:
├─ Current model: 8 regional service centers, each with minimum staff
│  ├─ Fixed cost per center: $1M/year (rent, management, equipment)
│  ├─ Total fixed overhead: $8M/year
│  ├─ Revenue per center: $5M (on average)
│  ├─ Margin required to break even: $8M / $40M = 20% (can't achieve)
│
├─ Competitor model: 2 centralized hubs + mobile workforce
│  ├─ Fixed cost: $2M/year (hubs)
│  ├─ Variable cost: Higher (mileage, real-time dispatch coordination)
│  ├─ Revenue same: $40M
│  ├─ Margin required: ~12% (achievable)
│
└─ Result: You have 4x the fixed overhead per dollar of revenue; can't compete on price

ROOT CAUSE HYPOTHESIS #4: PRODUCT / SERVICE LINE DETERIORATION
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

What it means:
├─ Specific service lines (product categories) are unprofitable and dragging down unit
├─ Some service lines are commoditized; others are still defensible
├─ Cost-cutting = cutting uniform across unit; should be cutting by service line
├─ Some service lines should be exited entirely; others should be scaled

Red flags for this cause:
├─ Margin analysis by service line shows 2–3 lines are highly profitable, rest are negative
├─ Unprofitable lines are declining anyway (market is shrinking)
├─ Profitable lines are growing (market opportunity is here, not there)
├─ Unit is "bundling" unprofitable service with profitable ones (customers want bundled service)
├─ Competitors have exited unprofitable lines; you're hanging on (hoping for recovery)
├─ Service lines require different go-to-market (sales, pricing, customer base), not unified
├─ Consolidation opportunity: Small teams doing similar work across multiple service lines
└─ Automation potential: Some service lines can be partially automated; others can't

Example:
├─ Service line A (Preventive maintenance): 30% of revenue, 8% margin
│  ├─ Commodity market; pricing pressure from competitors and customers
│  ├─ High fixed cost (technician base, scheduling, customer relationships)
│  ├─ Declining order book (customers self-servicing)
│  └─ Recommendation: Exit or radically restructure (move to lower-touch, lower-cost model)
│
├─ Service line B (Emergency/reactive repair): 40% of revenue, -5% margin
│  ├─ Customers expect fast response (drives high cost)
│  ├─ Pricing power is weak ("emergency" doesn't justify premium price in customer minds)
│  ├─ Demand is volatile (can't plan staffing)
│  └─ Recommendation: Restructure pricing (customer pays for speed/guarantee) or exit
│
├─ Service line C (Specialized technical services): 20% of revenue, 22% margin
│  ├─ High-skilled technicians (scarce, expensive, good margin)
│  ├─ Customers willing to pay premium (mission-critical, differentiated)
│  ├─ Growing demand (customers need more specialization)
│  └─ Recommendation: Scale this; invest in talent, pricing
│
└─ Service line D (Asset management / monitoring): 10% of revenue, -2% margin
   ├─ Tech-enabled service (software + hardware)
   ├─ Customer expectations: 24/7 availability, real-time alerts
   ├─ Current delivery model: Manual monitoring (can't meet customer expectations, unprofitable)
   └─ Recommendation: Either transform to tech platform (invest) or exit

ROOT CAUSE HYPOTHESIS #5: EXECUTION / OPERATIONAL EXCELLENCE ISSUES
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

What it means:
├─ Pricing and customer mix might be OK, but operational execution is poor
├─ High rework, waste, inefficiency, or overstaffing is destroying margins
├─ Unit has lost discipline in cost control / operational rigor
├─ Best managers leaving = management depth missing = execution quality declining
├─ Culture of "do whatever it takes to win the deal" has eroded margins

Red flags for this cause:
├─ Rework/quality metrics are high vs. competitors
├─ Labor utilization rates are low (too much non-billable time)
├─ Absenteeism/turnover is high (team is disengaged, burned out)
├─ Project cost overruns are common (schedule slips, scope creep)
├─ Customer complaints about service quality are increasing
├─ Inventory waste is high (dead stock, shrink)
├─ Procurement is inefficient (not getting competitive pricing)
└─ Best performers are leaving (those who care about quality/standards)

ROOT CAUSE HYPOTHESIS #6: MARKET / EXTERNAL STRUCTURAL DECLINE
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

What it means:
├─ The industrial-services market itself is in decline
├─ Customer demand has shifted (they need different services, or less service)
├─ Disruption has changed what customers buy (automation, insourcing, different service models)
├─ Unit is in a shrinking market; no cost-cutting will fix market decline

Red flags for this cause:
├─ Entire market is declining (not just your unit; competitors also losing share)
├─ Customer base is shrinking (consolidation, automation, outsourcing)
├─ New entrants are disrupting (gig model, tech platforms, direct-to-consumer)
├─ Price compression is industry-wide (not just your pricing problem)
├─ Order book is declining across all service lines (not specific to weak lines)
├─ Winning new customers is increasingly hard (even after price cuts)
├─ Customer churn is accelerating (customers going direct, to competitors, or reducing spend)
├─ Technology displacement (robots, AI, IoT are replacing manual industrial services)
└─ Best customers' economics are deteriorating (they're buying less because their economics are bad)

Example:
├─ Industrial base in your region has been declining 3–5% annually for 10 years
├─ Manufacturing customers are automating (fewer breakdowns, less maintenance)
├─ New service model (predictive maintenance via IoT) is replacing reactive maintenance
├─ Your unit is still offering reactive 24/7 maintenance (expensive, low demand)
├─ All competitors are in same situation (but some are pivoting to tech-enabled services)

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
```

### 1.2 Diagnostic Roadmap: 60-Day Root Cause Assessment

**Goal:** Move from hypothesis to fact-based diagnosis of where losses are coming from. This is non-negotiable; don't proceed with turnaround plan without clear diagnosis.

```
PHASE 1: DATA COLLECTION & SEGMENTATION (Days 1–20)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Activity 1.1: Gross Margin Analysis by Customer & Service Line
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Pull data from finance/operations:
├─ Revenue by customer (last 24 months)
├─ Direct cost of service by customer (labor, materials, subcontracts)
├─ Gross margin by customer (revenue - direct costs) / revenue
├─ Service lines associated with each customer (many customers use multiple services)
├─ Revenue by service line (isolated from customer data)
├─ Direct cost by service line
├─ Gross margin by service line

Output: Two matrices:
├─ Matrix A: Customer profitability map
│  ├─ Rank 50 largest customers by revenue
│  ├─ Show gross margin for each
│  ├─ Identify customers with negative or <5% margin
│  ├─ Identify customers with >25% margin (your profitable anchor customers)
│  └─ Show trend (margin improving/declining year over year)
│
└─ Matrix B: Service line profitability map
   ├─ Rank service lines by revenue
   ├─ Show gross margin for each
   ├─ Identify unprofitable service lines (negative or <10% margin)
   ├─ Identify profitable service lines (>20% margin)
   └─ Show trend (growing/declining)

Key insight: If 20% of customers = 100% of profit, then problem is customer mix + pricing.
             If service lines show wide variance (some +30%, some -10%), problem is portfolio mix.
             If all customers/lines show declining margins, problem is either pricing or delivery model.

Activity 1.2: Customer Concentration & Churn Analysis
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Pull data:
├─ Top 20 customers: Revenue, margin, whether they've grown, shrunk, or stayed flat
├─ Customer wins in last 24 months: How many, at what size, with what terms
├─ Customer losses in last 24 months: How many, at what size, for what reasons
├─ Customer churn rate: Count of customers lost / average active customer base
├─ Reason for churn (interview sales team, account managers):
│  ├─ Price (customer found cheaper alternative)
│  ├─ Service quality (customer dissatisfied with service)
│  ├─ Competitor displacement (lost to specific competitor)
│  ├─ Customer consolidation/closure (customer went out of business or merged)
│  ├─ Insourcing (customer decided to do in-house instead)
│  └─ Not specified (customer stopped buying, no clear reason)
│
└─ High-value customer retention: Separate analysis for top 25 customers
   ├─ How many have been with you 5+ years (sticky)
   ├─ How many were gained in last 3 years (new wins)
   ├─ Churn trend: Are you losing high-value or low-value customers?

Key insight: If losing high-value customers to price, you have pricing problem + possibly delivery problem.
             If high churn but low deflection, you have customer satisfaction/market problem.
             If new customer wins aren't sticking, you have sales/onboarding problem.

Activity 1.3: Pricing vs. Market Analysis
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Research competitor pricing:
├─ For each service line, identify 3–5 key competitors
├─ Research/request pricing for identical service scope
├─ Compare your pricing to competitor pricing (percentage difference)
├─ For customers you've lost, ask: "What did competitor quote you?"
├─ For customers you've won, ask: "What did you expect to pay vs. what we quoted?"

Output:
├─ Pricing vs. market sheet:
│  ├─ Service line A: You $100/hour; Market: $130/hour (30% BELOW market = pricing problem)
│  ├─ Service line B: You $80/hour; Market: $80/hour (AT market = execution problem if unprofitable)
│  ├─ Service line C: You $200/hour; Market: $180/hour (10% ABOVE market but profitable = differentiated)
│  └─ Service line D: You $60/hour; Market: $90/hour (33% BELOW market = likely dumping)
│
└─ Pricing history (pull from CRM):
   ├─ When were prices last increased?
   ├─ Were increases across the board or by customer?
   ├─ How much resistance to price increases?
   └─ Are old customers locked in at old rates?

Key insight: If your pricing is 20–30% below market, root cause is clear: PRICING PROBLEM.
             If pricing is at market but margins are negative, root cause is DELIVERY/EXECUTION PROBLEM.

Activity 1.4: Customer Switching Cost & Stickiness Analysis
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

For top 20 customers, assess:
├─ How integrated is your service into their operations?
│  ├─ Critical (customer depends on you to operate): Switching cost = HIGH
│  ├─ Important (customer would be disrupted but could manage): Switching cost = MEDIUM
│  ├─ Useful (customer could easily replace with competitor): Switching cost = LOW
│
├─ How long have they been customers? (Longer = more integrated = higher switching cost)
├─ How many internal resources do they dedicate to managing relationship?
├─ Do they use your service for multiple needs (bundled) or single need (commoditized)?
├─ What would it cost them to switch? (Time, disruption, training, qualification of new vendor)
└─ Is there contractual lock-in? (Long-term contracts, penalties for early termination)

Key insight: High-switching-cost customers should be protected (priority for retention, price increases reasonable).
             Low-switching-cost customers are vulnerable to churn (need service excellence or pricing advantage).

Activity 1.5: Overhead & Fixed Cost Analysis
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Pull from finance:
├─ Headcount by function (sales, operations, management, admin)
├─ Headcount by location (regional centers, field, corporate)
├─ Headcount trend (how many people were there 3 years ago, now)
├─ Compensation costs (wages, benefits, overhead)
├─ Fixed costs by location: Rent, utilities, facilities, insurance
├─ Fixed costs by function: Corporate allocation, shared services
├─ Fixed costs that vary with revenue (proportional) vs. fixed costs (lump sum)

Output:
├─ Fixed cost as % of revenue:
│  ├─ 3 years ago: Fixed cost = $X, Revenue = $Y, Ratio = X/Y
│  ├─ Today: Fixed cost = $X', Revenue = $Y', Ratio = X'/Y' (likely HIGHER if revenue declined)
│  └─ Indicates: Revenue declined but fixed costs didn't → margin compression
│
├─ Overhead per customer (by size):
│  ├─ Average large customer: $800K revenue, needs dedicated account manager + support (overhead = $100K)
│  ├─ Average medium customer: $200K revenue, needs part-time support (overhead = $20K)
│  ├─ Average small customer: $50K revenue, minimal overhead support (overhead = $5K)
│  └─ Indicates: If customer base has shifted to smaller customers, overhead per customer is too high
│
├─ Delivery cost by model:
│  ├─ On-call/responsive service: High fixed cost (minimum crew, ready to respond)
│  ├─ Scheduled/contracted service: Medium fixed cost (crews scheduled, not always on-call)
│  ├─ Project-based service: Low fixed cost (crews assigned as needed)
│  └─ Indicates: If customer demand has shifted from scheduled to transactional, your model is misaligned
│
└─ Utilization rates (by location/team):
   ├─ Field technician utilization: What % of their time is billable to customer (vs. travel, admin, training)?
   ├─ If <70%, you have overhead problem (costs too high for revenue generated)
   ├─ If 50–60%, you have model problem (can't achieve profitability with this model)
   └─ Benchmark: Profitable service businesses run at 75–85% utilization

Key insight: If fixed costs have stayed flat while revenue declined 20%, margin compression is explained.
             If customer base has shifted to smaller customers, overhead per customer is too high.
             If utilization rates are <70%, delivery model needs restructuring.

DELIVERABLE (Day 20): Root Cause Hypothesis Summary
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Based on Phase 1 data, rank the root causes:

1. PRIMARY DRIVER (the #1 thing causing losses):
   ├─ If customer margin analysis shows 20% of customers = 100% of profit, and unit is chasing volume in low-margin
   │  customer base → PRIMARY DRIVER = CUSTOMER MIX & PRICING
   │
   ├─ If service line analysis shows 2–3 lines are profitable and rest are underwater → PRIMARY DRIVER = PORTFOLIO MIX
   │
   ├─ If pricing is 20–30% below market → PRIMARY DRIVER = PRICING PROBLEM
   │
   ├─ If pricing is at market but utilization is <70% and fixed costs are high → PRIMARY DRIVER = DELIVERY MODEL
   │
   └─ If all metrics show decline (shrinking market, declining margins, declining volume) → PRIMARY DRIVER = MARKET DECLINE
       (This is the hardest to fix; exit may be only option)

2. SECONDARY DRIVERS (contributing factors):
   ├─ Execution issues (rework, inefficiency, waste)
   ├─ Organizational decay (best managers leaving, culture deteriorating)
   ├─ Technology lag (competitors have platforms, you don't)
   └─ Product mix (unprofitable service lines need to be exited)

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PHASE 2: DEEP DIVE BY ROOT CAUSE (Days 21–45)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Based on Phase 1 diagnosis, execute deep dive:

IF PRIMARY DRIVER = CUSTOMER MIX & PRICING:
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Activity 2.1: Repricing opportunity analysis
├─ For each profitable customer segment, model: "What if we raised prices by 10%, 15%, 20%?"
├─ Estimate churn impact (how many customers would leave at each price increase?)
├─ Calculate net revenue impact (revenue increase minus churn loss)
├─ Example:
│  ├─ Segment A (high-switching-cost customers): 20 customers, $800K avg revenue, 40% gross margin
│  │  ├─ Current total: $16M revenue, $6.4M gross profit
│  │  ├─ If raise price 15%, lose 1 customer (5% churn):
│  │  │  ├─ New total: $16M * 1.15 * 0.95 = $17.48M revenue
│  │  │  ├─ New profit (40% margin): $6.99M gross profit
│  │  │  ├─ Gain: +$600K gross profit from single price move
│  │  └─ Recommendation: EXECUTE this price increase (customers can tolerate it; high switching cost protects you)
│  │
│  └─ Segment B (price-sensitive customers): 60 customers, $200K avg revenue, 12% gross margin
│     ├─ Current total: $12M revenue, $1.44M gross profit
│     ├─ If raise price 10%, lose 10% of customers (6 customers):
│     │  ├─ New total: $12M * 1.10 * 0.90 = $11.88M revenue
│     │  ├─ New profit (15% margin, improved by consolidation): $1.78M
│     │  ├─ Gain: +$340K gross profit (but lost 6 customers)
│     │  └─ Recommendation: SELECTIVE reprice + consolidate operations (exit lowest-margin customers to improve overall mix)
│     │
│     └─ Alternative: Exit lowest-margin customers in segment (30 customers, $100K avg, 5% margin)
│        ├─ Revenue impact: -$3M
│        ├─ Profit impact: -$150K (they were barely breaking even)
│        ├─ But reduces overhead allocation to remaining customers → improves overall margin to 15%
│        └─ Recommendation: PRUNE customer base; focus on profitable accounts

Activity 2.2: Customer segment profitability mapping
├─ Identify customer segments (by industry, size, geography, service mix)
├─ Calculate segment-level metrics:
│  ├─ Revenue, gross margin, contribution margin (gross margin - allocated overhead)
│  ├─ Churn rate, NPS, switching cost
│  ├─ Competitive intensity (how many competitors do they buy from?)
│  └─ Growth potential (expanding or contracting customers?)
│
└─ Rank segments by profit and opportunity:
   ├─ TIER 1 (Defend & Grow): Profitable, sticky, growing → increase prices 10–15%; invest in growth
   ├─ TIER 2 (Optimize & Consolidate): Profitable but slow-growing → increase prices 5–10%; consolidate to improve efficiency
   ├─ TIER 3 (Restructure or Exit): Unprofitable or barely profitable → either restructure (new pricing/model) or exit
   └─ TIER 4 (Exit): Unprofitable, low margin, declining → EXIT; reallocate overhead to profitable segments

IF PRIMARY DRIVER = DELIVERY MODEL / FIXED COSTS:
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Activity 2.3: Service delivery model redesign
├─ Current model: Describe how service is currently delivered (staffing, locations, response model, customer interaction)
├─ Cost structure: Fixed costs per location, variable costs per service delivery

│  │  ├─ Gross profit: $7.2M
│  │  ├─ Contribution after fixed costs: $5.2M (best leverage)
